[Table](?path=/docs/components-table--docs) for comparing rows, [Tree](?path=/docs/components-tree--docs) for deeper hierarchy, [Related](?path=/docs/patterns-related--docs) for a record card, and [Collapsible](?path=/docs/components-collapsible--docs) for a whole section.

Sources: [shadcn Item](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/components/base/item), [Base UI useRender](https://base-ui.com/react/utils/use-render). Ledger keeps its aligned record rows and separate actions as a product extension.

<!-- page: Components/Kbd (src/stories/components/Kbd.mdx) -->

# Kbd

Keyboard input displayed as a keycap, in text, tooltips and menu hints. Use `KbdShortcut`
for a shortcut written once for every platform (`"Mod+K"` is ⌘ K on a Mac and Ctrl K
elsewhere), and `KbdGroup` to compose the caps of a shortcut by hand. The existing
`Kbd.Group` alias also works.

_Example: story `Stories.KbdMatrix`._

## Anatomy

All three parts render native `<kbd>` elements and accept their native props and refs.
`Kbd` draws a 16px-tall cap, at least 16px wide, using the sunken surface, default
border, extra-small radius and small text tokens. `KbdGroup` and `KbdShortcut` space
their caps 4px apart.

```tsx
import { Kbd, KbdGroup, KbdShortcut } from "@ledger/design-system";

<KbdShortcut keys="Mod+K" />

<KbdGroup>
  <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>
  <Kbd>[</Kbd>
</KbdGroup>
```

Use separate caps when that makes a multi-key shortcut easier to read.

## Shortcuts on every platform

Write a shortcut once, as keys joined by `+`, with `Mod` for the platform's modifier:
`"Mod+K"`, `"Mod+Shift+P"`, `"Ctrl+["`, `"Escape"`. `Mod` is Command on macOS, iOS and
iPadOS and Control elsewhere. `KbdShortcut` draws the keys in the platform's glyphs and
order (⇧⌘P on a Mac, Ctrl Shift P elsewhere), capitalizes a single character, and names the
named keys once: the arrows, Enter (↵), Escape (Esc), Tab, Space, Backspace and Delete.
Use `Mod` for a chord that follows the platform, and `Ctrl` for one that is Control
everywhere, like the side nav's Ctrl [; on Apple platforms Control is drawn ⌃, so it
reads ⌃ [ there.

_Example: story `Stories.Shortcuts`._

The platform is read once for the page, and every shortcut in the kit reads the same
answer:

- **`useModifierKey()`** for a render: `"meta"` or `"ctrl"`. The server and the first
  client render say `"ctrl"`, so hydration matches; the browser's answer follows straight
  after. `KbdShortcut` uses it.
- **`getModifierKey()`** for a key handler, which runs in the browser: test `event.metaKey`
  when it says `"meta"` and `event.ctrlKey` when it says `"ctrl"`.
- **`useFormatShortcut()`** returns a function that gives a shortcut as a string, following
  the locale and the platform: `format("Mod+K")` is the text for a hint or a title ("⌘K",
  "Ctrl+K"), `format("Mod+K", "label")` what a screen reader says ("Command K"), and
  `format("Mod+K", "aria")` the value for `aria-keyshortcuts` on the control the shortcut
  runs ("Meta+K"). `formatShortcut(shortcut, { modifier, messages, as })` is the same,
  pure, for code outside React; in a render, prefer the hook, which hydrates safely.
- **`shortcutKeys(shortcut, options)`** gives each key's cap, spoken name and
  `aria-keyshortcuts` name, for a caller that draws its own.

Pass `modifier` to show one platform's keys regardless of the reader's, as documentation
does. The kit draws shortcuts; binding one to an action stays with the caller.

_Example: story `Stories.PlatformModifier`._

## Accessibility

`<kbd>` marks up keyboard input. Caps and groups have no built-in focus or activation
behavior; the surrounding button or menu item owns the action. Keep the action's name
in the surrounding text, such as “Press Command K to search.”

`KbdShortcut` hides its caps from assistive technology and adds one visually hidden line
with the keys' names ("Shift Command P"), so a screen reader never reads a glyph's
character name. Put `aria-keyshortcuts` (from `useFormatShortcut`) on the control the
shortcut runs.

On `Kbd`, `label` sets the glyph's `aria-label`; an explicit `aria-label` takes precedence.
ARIA does not name an element with no role, so screen readers may read the glyph itself;
for a glyph key, prefer `KbdShortcut`. The shortcut should remain understandable from its
visible text and context.

Key names and word caps come from the locale's messages (`keyCommand`, `keyControl`,
`keyCapControl` and the rest), so a German product shows Strg and says Steuerung.

## Props

`className`, `style`, attributes, events and `ref` target each part's own `<kbd>`.
All refs use `HTMLElement`. Parts expose `data-slot="kbd"`, `data-slot="kbd-group"` and
`data-slot="kbd-shortcut"`; a shortcut also carries `data-modifier`, the platform it drew.

_Props: generated from `Kbd`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Props: generated from `KbdShortcut`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

### Playground

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

## Migration

Existing `Kbd`, `label`, and `Kbd.Group` callers need no edits. For a shortcut that follows
the platform, replace a hand-written `⌘` or `Ctrl` cap with `KbdShortcut keys="Mod+…"`.

# KeyValue

One rail row: a label column and a value. Owner, Frequency, Last verified, each on its own line with the label in a fixed column so the values make a column too. On its own it is a definition list of one pair, valid wherever it sits; a rail's rows go in one **KeyValue.Group**, which makes them one definition list and gives them one label width.

It is one of two ways to write a fact. A [Fact](?path=/docs/components-fact--docs) is inline, label then value on one baseline, for the strip under a record's title; a KeyValue is a row, for the rail and the inspector.

_Example: story `Stories.KeyValueMatrix`._

## Anatomy

| Part  | What it is                                                                                                                             |
| ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Label | `dt` in the label column, `labelWidth` wide (104 by default, or the group's), `font.body` in `color.text.subtle`. A label that is cut shows in full in a tooltip on hover. |
| Value | `dd` in the rest, `font.body` in `color.text`: text, a Badge, a Person, a TextLink, an Absent. Truncates unless `wrap`, which also breaks an unbroken identifier or timestamp inside the rail (the Unbroken story). A cut value, plain or composed (a code and a title, a TextLink), shows its whole text in a tooltip on hover and when a control inside it takes keyboard focus, through [Truncate](?path=/docs/components-truncate--docs). It truncates across only, so a control in the value keeps its focus ring and touch area above and below the row (the Control In A Value story). |
| Row   | `space.050` above and below, `space.150` between label and value, baselines aligned.                                                   |

## Variants

KeyValue has one appearance. What varies is the value:

| The value              | Use               |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- |
| A word, a name, a date | Text.             |
| A state                | A Badge.          |
| A person               | A Person.         |
| A record               | A TextLink.       |
| A statement            | Text with `wrap`. |
| Nothing                | An Absent.        |

Not built, and why: an editable value, because that is an [Editable](?path=/docs/patterns-editable--docs) inside the value; a named width scale, because the label widths in use are still being settled.

## KeyValue.Group

One `dl` for a rail, an inspector group or a row's More fields. Its KeyValues become its rows (a `div` holding the `dt` and `dd`, which HTML allows), share its `labelWidth` through context, and follow its `layout`:

| `layout`         | Rows                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auto` (default) | Label beside value while the value has at least 8rem beside the label; label over value when the group is narrower (a phone, a narrow panel). Every row changes together, because every row has the same width and the same label and value bases. It is intrinsic layout (a wrapping row), so it responds to the group's own width, not the window. |
| `columns`        | Label beside value at any width: a rail of one-line rows.                                                                                                  |
| `stacked`        | Label over value, always.                                                                                                                                  |

A row's own `labelWidth` overrides the group's; give the width to the group once instead. A screen reader hears one list of pairs instead of one list per fact. The group ends at each value: a KeyValue inside a value (a peek's facts, a HoverCard's) is its own definition list again (the Group Ends At The Value story).

_Example: story `Stories.Group`._

_Example: story `Stories.GroupInANarrowPanel`._

_Example: story `Stories.GroupLayouts`._

_Example: story `Stories.GroupEndsAtTheValue`._

## Sizes

One size, `font.body`. The row is as wide as its rail; the label column is `labelWidth`, the same for every row in one rail, and the value takes the rest. The Glance uses 88, a rail 104; a rail with long labels ("Authorizing official") sets 160 on its KeyValue.Group.

_Example: story `Stories.InRail`._

## States

A KeyValue has one state. Its value may: a Badge is a state, a TextLink hovers. The row does not.

## Modifiers

- **`labelWidth`**: the label column, the same down one rail; on the KeyValue.Group once.
- **`wrap`** for a value that is a sentence.
- **The value** as in Variants.

## Content

- **The label is a noun**, one or two words, no colon: "Owner", "Last verified", "Next due". The column is the colon.
- **The value is one thing.** Two facts are two rows.
- **Nothing there is an Absent**, not an empty row and not "N/A", which is a different fact.
- **The order is the order the reader asks:** who, how often, when last, when next, then the rest.

## Style

| Element | Token                                                               |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Label   | `font.body` · `color.text.subtle` · `labelWidth` column             |
| Value   | `font.body` · `color.text`                                          |
| Row     | `space.050` block · `space.150` between columns · baselines aligned |

## Accessibility

- **It is a definition list**: `dl`, `dt`, `dd`, so a screen reader hears "Owner, Dana Whitfield" as a pair. In a KeyValue.Group a rail is one list of pairs.
- **A cut label or value shows its whole text** in a tooltip on hover, and a cut value on keyboard focus of a control inside it. The tooltip is a visual copy: the full text is in the DOM and read by a screen reader. A value that matters whole takes `wrap`, so no one has to hover; a touch screen has no hover.
- **A control in the value stays whole on the block axis.** The value clips only sideways (`overflow-x: clip` with the ellipsis), so an [Editable](?path=/docs/patterns-editable--docs) or a [TextLink](?path=/docs/components-textlink--docs) keeps its focus ring and, where a pointer is coarse, a touch area at least 24px tall.
- **The label is text, not a heading.** A rail's sections are headed by an Eyebrow or a Collapsible; the label names one fact.
- **Contrast:** the label in `color.text.subtle` passes 4.5:1; the gate runs the matrix.

_Example: story `Stories.ControlInAValue`._

_Example: story `Stories.CutValueAndLabel`._

## Props

Native props and refs target the row's root: the `dl` on its own, the row `div` inside a KeyValue.Group. Use IDs, data attributes and event handlers directly; `className` merges with the default row classes, and caller `style` can override the columns computed from `labelWidth`. The inner `dt`/`dd`, wrapping behavior and the reveal of a cut label or value are preserved.

_Props: generated from `KeyValue`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

### KeyValue.Group

Native `dl` props, a ref and `render` target the group's list.

_Props: generated from `KeyValue.Group`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

# LinkButton

Navigation that looks like a button: “View requirements”, “Create program” when it opens a page, “Open my work”. LinkButton is an anchor, or the application's router Link through `render`, with [Button](?path=/docs/components-button--docs)'s variants, sizes, icon slots and insets. Because it is a real link, the reader can middle-click it, copy its address or open it in a new tab, and Base UI's native-button check never sees it. LinkIconButton is its icon-only form.

Use Button for an action that happens on this page, and [TextLink](?path=/docs/components-textlink--docs) for a link inside a sentence or a record name in a table. A Button that navigates from `onClick`, or a Button that renders a router Link, is the mistake this part replaces.

_Example: story `Stories.Matrix`._

## Variants and sizes

| Variant     | Use                                                                   |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `secondary` | The default: a destination beside other actions.                     |
| `primary`   | The main destination of a region, such as Continue to review.        |
| `subtle`    | A low-emphasis destination in a toolbar, a row or a card footer.      |
| `danger`    | A destination that leads to a destructive task, rarely.               |

Sizes are Button's: `medium` 32px (the default), `small` 28px and `xsmall` 24px. `iconBefore` and `iconAfter` take an icon element, drawn at 14px and hidden from assistive technology, and the icon's side takes the smaller inset. `isFullWidth` fills the container. There is no `link` variant: a link that looks like text is a TextLink.

## Router links

Pass the router's Link through `render`. It keeps its href, its client-side navigation and its active state; LinkButton supplies the look, the icons and the children. A custom component must forward the props and the ref it receives to its anchor.

```tsx
import { Link } from "@tanstack/react-router";
import { LinkButton } from "@ledger/design-system";

<LinkButton variant="primary" iconBefore={<Plus />} render={<Link to="/programs/new" />}>
  Create program
</LinkButton>;
```

TanStack Router's `createLink(LinkButton)` works too, and gives a component that takes the router's `to`, `params` and `search` directly. A router marks a link to the current page with `aria-current="page"`; that is right for a LinkButton that points at the page the reader is on.

_Example: story `Stories.RouterLink`._

## LinkIconButton

The icon-only form, with a required `label` that names the destination and shows in its tooltip on hover and keyboard focus, as on [IconButton](?path=/docs/components-iconbutton--docs). `small` is 28px, the default, and `medium` 32px with a 16px icon. Where any pointer is coarse it takes a hit area of at least 24px. Say where it goes, including a new tab: “Open CTRL-0412 in a new tab”. `isTooltipDisabled` drops the tooltip when the label is already visible nearby.

_Example: story `Stories.IconOnly`._

## Disabled with a reason

A destination that is not ready takes `disabledReason`. The link loses its href and stays in the tab order as a disabled link (`role="link"`, `aria-disabled="true"`), so a keyboard reader reaches it and learns why: the reason is its accessible description and shows in a tooltip on hover, on keyboard focus and on a tap. Clicks and Enter do nothing. While a reason is set the `render` element is not rendered, only its children, so a router link cannot navigate or appear in the browser's link menu. On LinkIconButton the tooltip shows the label and then the reason.

Prefer a destination that is always available and explains on arrival; use a reason when following the link would only lead to an error.

_Example: story `Stories.DisabledWithAReason`._

A reason that comes or goes while the link has focus leaves focus on it: a report that becomes ready while the reader is on View report gets its href and router link back, and Enter follows it.

_Example: story `Stories.ReasonChangesWhileFocused`._

## Accessibility

- It is a link: Tab reaches it, Enter follows it, and Space does not, as for any link. A screen reader announces a link, so the label names a destination (“View requirements”), not an operation (“Save”).
- An external or new-tab destination says so in its label, or in a visible icon with the words in `label` for LinkIconButton.
- The icons are decorative; the name comes from the children or `label`.
- The focus ring, the hit area on touch and the disabled face are Button's.

## Props

_Props: generated from `LinkButton`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

### LinkIconButton

_Props: generated from `LinkIconButton`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

# List

Bulleted and numbered lists on one inset and two spacings: validation messages, conflicts, the steps of an instruction, the points of a narrative. The marker hangs in the inset, so each item's text lines up with the text above the list. It is a real `ul` or `ol`, so a screen reader says how many items there are.

```tsx
<List>
  <List.Item>Choose a profile.</List.Item>
  <List.Item>Add at least one system.</List.Item>
</List>
```

_Example: story `Stories.ListMatrix`._

## When to use it

- **Two or more short points** a reader should see as separate: what is missing before a program can be created, the conflicts in a selection.
- **`ordered`** when the order matters (steps, a ranking, an order the text refers to); bullets otherwise.
- **`spacing="loose"`** when items are sentences or wrap; `tight`, the default, for short lines.
- **Not for records.** A list of records a reader opens or acts on is an [Item.Group](?path=/docs/components-item--docs), a [Timeline](?path=/docs/components-timeline--docs) or a DataTable.
- **Not for facts.** Labelled values are [KeyValue](?path=/docs/components-keyvalue--docs) rows in a KeyValue.Group.
- **Authored Markdown** renders its lists through this part: [Prose](?path=/docs/components-typography--docs) with `markdown`.

_Example: story `Stories.Semantics`._

## Anatomy

| Part      | What it is                                                                                                                    |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| List      | `ul` (`list-disc`, `space.200` inset) or `ol` with `ordered` (`list-decimal`, `space.300` inset, for two-digit numbers). The inset is logical: it moves to the right in a right-to-left locale. |
| List.Item | `li`, `space.025` from its marker; it wraps and breaks a long word rather than running past the list.                         |
| Spacing   | `space.025` between items when `tight`, `space.100` when `loose`.                                                            |

The list takes its size and colour from where it sits: an Alert's description, a Field's error, a paragraph's size. `start` numbers an ordered list from where the text left off. A List inside a List.Item nests.

_Example: story `Stories.InAnAlert`._

## Accessibility

- **A list is announced as a list** with its count, and each item as one of that count. Bullets typed into text are read as characters.
- **Markers are drawn by CSS**, so they are not read as words.
- **Links in items** are TextLinks; an item that is a whole record is not a list item but an Item.

## Props

### List

_Props: generated from `List`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

### List.Item

_Props: generated from `ListItem`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

# Locale

**LedgerProvider** gives every part under it the reader's locale, time zone and writing direction, and the kit's own words. Every date, number and label a part shows goes through it: DateTime, RelativeTime and DateLabel, DataTable's `c.date`, the Calendar's first day of the week, a typed day in a DatePicker, Pagination's words, Shell's landmark names. Mount one near the root, with the reader's zone.

_Example: story `Stories.ReadersZone`._

## At the root

```tsx
import { LedgerProvider, ModeProvider, Toaster } from "@ledger/design-system";

<ModeProvider>
  <LedgerProvider locale="en-US" timeZone={readerTimeZone}>
    <App />
    <Toaster />
  </LedgerProvider>
</ModeProvider>;
```

The provider renders one element around its children, carrying `lang` from `locale` and `dir` from `direction`. Parts that draw in a portal outside it and depend on direction, such as the Toaster, a Combobox popup, the Calendar and a chart's tooltip, read it from the provider instead.

| Option      | Without it                             | What it decides                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `locale`    | `en-US`, never the host's              | A BCP 47 tag: the words and numerals of dates and numbers, plural rules, 12- or 24-hour clocks, the first day of the week, and how a typed day or time reads. |
| `timeZone`  | `UTC`                                  | The IANA zone instants show in, such as `America/New_York`. A calendar day never shifts, whatever the zone.                                                   |
| `direction` | `ltr`                                  | `rtl` for a right-to-left language.                                                                                                                           |
| `messages`  | The English words in `defaultMessages` | The kit's labels, announcements and templates, by key. Pass a module constant: a new object on every render rebuilds the formatters.                          |

A nested provider inherits every option it does not set, and merges its `messages` over its parent's, so a region can take another zone or a few other words without repeating the rest.

## Days and instants

An ISO day (`"2026-09-18"`) is a calendar day: a due date, a milestone. It reads the same day everywhere. An instant (an ISO timestamp with an offset, a `Date`, epoch milliseconds) is a point in time, shown in the provider's zone, so the same instant is the evening of Sep 18 in Los Angeles and the morning of Sep 19 in Tokyo. Without a `timeZone`, every instant shows in UTC, and an evening entered in the Americas reads as the next day.

_Example: story `Stories.InstantsAndDays`._

## The same on the server and the client

Pass the same locale and zone to the provider on the server and on the client, or the markup will not match on hydration. The server knows the reader's zone only when the product stores it, as an account preference or a cookie; pass the stored value on both sides. Otherwise render the server's zone first and take the reader's once the client has hydrated:

```tsx
import { useSyncExternalStore } from "react";

const subscribe = () => () => {};
const readerZone = () => Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone;

/** The reader's zone on the client, and `serverZone` while rendering on the server and hydrating. */
export function useReaderTimeZone(serverZone = "UTC") {
  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, readerZone, () => serverZone);
}
```

React renders the server snapshot during hydration, then renders again with the client's, so the first paint matches the server and the dates settle into the reader's zone straight after. Never read the host's locale or zone during a server render.

## Formatters in your own code

Show a date with DateTime, RelativeTime or DateLabel, and a date column with `c.date`. Where no part fits, such as an export, a message you `announce`, or a document title, `useLedgerLocale()` returns the provider's formatters:

| Returns                                                        | For                                                                                                                             |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `formatDate(value, options?)`                                  | An instant (a `Date` or epoch milliseconds, not a string), in the provider's zone. `options` are `Intl.DateTimeFormat` options. |
| `formatDay(day, options?)`, `formatDayRange`                   | A calendar day `{ year, month, day }`, or two, never shifted.                                                                   |
| `formatCalendarDate(date, options?)`                           | A `Date` read as the local year, month and day it was picked on, such as a Calendar's, never shifted.                           |
| `formatTime(time, options?)`                                   | A wall-clock time `{ hour, minute }`, on the locale's clock.                                                                    |
| `formatRelative(value, now?, style?)`                          | "5 minutes ago", "tomorrow": `{ text, next }`, `next` being the milliseconds until the words change.                            |
| `formatNumber(value, options?)`                                | A number, with `Intl.NumberFormat` options.                                                                                     |
| `formatPlural(count, forms)`                                   | The form for a count, from `{ one, other }` and the locale's other categories, with `{count}`.                                  |
| `t(key, params?)`                                              | One of the kit's messages, with its `{name}` placeholders filled.                                                               |
| `zonedParts(value)`, `toInstant(day, time)`                    | The day and time an instant falls on in the zone, and the instant a day and time name there.                                    |
| `timeZoneName(value, style?)`                                  | The zone's name at an instant: "PDT", or "Pacific Daylight Time" with `"long"`.                                                 |
| `parseDay(text)`, `parseTime(text)`                            | A day or time typed in the locale's words, or `null`.                                                                           |
| `locale`, `timeZone`, `direction`, `hourCycle`, `weekStartsOn` | The resolved values.                                                                                                            |

`createLedgerLocale(options)` returns the same object without React, for server code, a worker or a test.

_Example: story `Stories.Formatters`._

## Messages

Every word the kit writes itself (Close, Clear filters, "2 of 3 records", "Sort by", the landmarks' names) is a message. `defaultMessages` lists every key with its English text. Translate a template whole, placeholders included, so the word order follows the language: `recordPosition` is `"{position} of {total} records"`. A part's own `label` prop still overrides one instance.

_Example: story `Stories.Messages`._

_Example: story `Stories.RightToLeft`._

# Mode

The colour mode: light, dark, or whatever the machine says. It is one attribute on the root, `data-color-mode`, and every token reads it, so the whole product flips at once and no component knows. The choice is the reader's, per browser, in `localStorage` under `ledger.color-mode`; never per account, so a shared machine keeps each person's choice. **`modeScript`** applies the stored choice before the first paint, **`ModeProvider`** owns it, **`ModeSwitch`** is the control.

It is the one setting that belongs to the document. Row [density](?path=/docs/components-density--docs) is a table's; the shell's widths are the shell's.

_Example: story `Stories.Live`._

## Anatomy

| Part           | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Attribute      | `data-color-mode="light"` or `"dark"` on the root pins a mode; no attribute lets `prefers-color-scheme` decide. `tokens.css` and `base.css` read it.                                                                        |
| Script         | `modeScript`: a string for the document head, above the stylesheet. It applies the stored choice before the first paint so nothing flashes. `modeScriptFor(key)` for another storage key.                                    |
| Provider       | `ModeProvider`: owns the choice. On mount it reads storage and applies it (a no-op after the script); every change is stored and applied at once. `useMode()` returns `{ mode, setMode, resolved }`, `resolved` being what is on screen. |
| Switch         | `ModeSwitch`: a ToggleGroup of three, sun, moon and monitor, `sm`. Icons only in chrome; `showLabels` in a settings form.                                                                                                |

## Variants

One control, in two forms. **Icons only**, in the top navigation's end, where the reader expects it and a label would be noise. **With labels**, `showLabels`, in a settings form, where the three words sit in a row of other settings.

There is no two-state form. A light-or-dark toggle has no answer for a machine that changes at dusk, and it pins a choice the reader never made; system is the default and the third state.

_Example: story `Stories.ControlledStory`._

## Sizes

One: the ToggleGroup's `sm`, 28px, the height of the chrome it sits in.

## States

| State    | Look                                                                                                                       |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Light    | The root pinned light; the sun is the selected item.                                                                       |
| Dark     | The root pinned dark; the moon.                                                                                            |
| System   | No attribute; the monitor. What is on screen follows the machine, and `resolved` says which.                               |
| Hover, focus, selected | The ToggleGroup's: the item tints, takes the kit's focus outline, and the selected one carries the selected fill. |

_Example: story `Stories.ModeMatrix`._

## Modifiers

- **`value` and `onChange`** on the switch override the provider, for a settings form that commits later, or for a story.
- **`showLabels`**, as in Variants.
- **`storageKey`** on the provider and **`modeScriptFor(key)`**, when a product keeps its own key. The two must agree.
- **`aria-label`** on the switch: "Appearance" by default.

## Content

- **The three words are Light, Dark and System.** Not "Match system", not "Auto", not "Night".
- **The switch's name is Appearance.** The reader is choosing how the product looks, not a "theme".
- **Never a colour by hand.** A hex value written into a component does not flip; every colour is a token, and the mode flips the tokens.
- **Never a mode-specific screen.** A page does not know which mode it is in; if a figure needs a different colour in dark, that colour is a token with two values.

## Style

| Element   | Token                                                                                              |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Switch    | The ToggleGroup, `sm`: `dimension.control.small` 28px · `dimension.icon.small` 14px              |
| Attribute | `data-color-mode` on `html` · every `color.*` and `elevation.*` token has a light and a dark value  |
| Motion    | None. A mode changes at once; a fade across every surface reads as a fault.                        |

## Accessibility

- **The switch is a group of toggle buttons** named Appearance. Each button has `aria-pressed` and an accessible name, including Light, Dark and System when only icons are visible.
- **Keyboard:** Tab enters and leaves the group as one stop; Left and Right move focus, and Space or Enter selects. The switch retains a selected mode when it is pressed again.
- **System honours the reader's machine,** including `prefers-color-scheme` set for a vision reason, so it is the default and never overridden by the product.
- **Contrast is tested in both modes:** every pairing on the Colour sheet, and the a11y gate runs each matrix in the mode the toolbar sets.
- **No flash:** the script marks the root before the first paint, so a reader who chose dark never sees a light page load.

## Props

_Props: generated from `ModeSwitch`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

The provider and the script, by hand:

| Export          | What it is                                                                                                  |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ModeProvider`  | Wraps the app; `storageKey` for a key of the product's own. Renders nothing itself.                         |
| `useMode()`     | `{ mode, setMode, resolved }`. Throws outside a provider.                                                   |
| `modeScript`    | The before-paint script for the default key; `modeScriptFor(key)` for another.                              |
| `readMode`, `writeMode`, `applyMode` | The three steps the provider takes, for a product that wires them itself.                  |

### Wiring it

Plain HTML: put the script in the head, above the stylesheet.

```html
<script>
  (function () {
    try {
      var m = localStorage.getItem("ledger.color-mode");
      if (m === "light" || m === "dark") document.documentElement.dataset.colorMode = m;
    } catch (e) {}
  })();
</script>
```

A framework with a `head()` hook renders the same string inline:

```tsx
import { modeScript, ModeProvider, ModeSwitch } from "@ledger/design-system";

head: () => ({ scripts: [{ children: modeScript }] });
// …
<ModeProvider>
  <Shell>
    <Shell.TopNav>
      …
      <Shell.TopNav.End>
        <ModeSwitch />
      </Shell.TopNav.End>
    </Shell.TopNav>
    …
  </Shell>
</ModeProvider>;
```

Do not also pin `data-color-mode` on the root in markup: the pin wins over the script and the switch cannot move it. Put `suppressHydrationWarning` on the `<html>` element: the script marks it before React hydrates, and React would otherwise report the mismatch.

### Playground

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

_Rendered in the Storybook: Controls._

- [Shell](?path=/docs/layout-shell--docs): where the switch sits, in the top navigation's end.
- [Density](?path=/docs/components-density--docs): the setting that is a table's, not the document's.

<!-- page: Components/NumberField (src/stories/components/NumberField.mdx) -->

# NumberField

A number the reader types or steps: a retention period, a budget, a count of reviewers. Base UI NumberField underneath, so the value is parsed and formatted in the reader's locale, kept within `min` and `max`, and stepped by `step` from the keyboard or the decrement and increment buttons.

Use it for a quantity. Do not use it for digits that name something, such as an identifier, a build number or a postcode: those are text, an [Input](?path=/docs/components-input--docs) with `inputMode="numeric"`, because a number field drops leading zeros, adds grouping separators and offers steps that mean nothing. For a value chosen along a range with a pointer, a slider may suit better; the kit has none yet.

_Example: story `Stories.Keyboard`._

## Stepping

| The reader                                | What happens                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Presses Up or Down                        | The value steps by `step` (1 by default).                               |
| Holds Shift, or Alt                       | It steps by `largeStep` (10), or `smallStep` (0.1).                     |
| Presses Home or End                       | It goes to `min` or `max`, when they are set.                           |
| Presses the decrement or increment button | It steps once; holding the button repeats.                              |
| Types                                     | The text is parsed in the locale; on blur it is formatted and clamped.  |
| Turns the wheel                           | Nothing, unless `allowWheelScrub`, and then only for the focused field. |

At a bound, the button that would pass it is unavailable. A read-only field keeps its value selectable and has no buttons. `onValueChange` runs on every change; `onValueCommitted` runs once the reader is done (on blur after typing, on releasing a button, at once for a key), which is the moment to save.

_Example: story `Stories.TypedAndFormatted`._
_Example: story `Stories.Wheel`._

## Formatting and locale

`format` takes `Intl.NumberFormat` options: a unit (`{ style: "unit", unit: "day", unitDisplay: "long" }` shows "90 days"), a currency, a percentage, fraction digits. The number is formatted and parsed in the closest `LedgerProvider`'s locale, not the browser's, so the server and the client agree; `locale` overrides it for one field. The value itself is always a plain number, or `null` when the field is empty, and a form receives the raw number under the Field's or the field's `name`.

Right to left, the buttons move to the field's end (the left), decrement nearest the number; Up still increases it.

_Example: story `Stories.Localized`._
_Example: story `Stories.RightToLeft`._
_Example: story `Stories.InAForm`._

## Sizes and states

`medium` (32px) in a form; `small` (28px) in a toolbar, a row or a rail. `className` and `style` go to the root, where the width is set, and `render` replaces the root element; the ref, `placeholder`, `autoFocus` and the `aria-*` props go to the input; `inputRef` is Base UI's hidden input that carries the value in a form.

_Example: story `Stories.States`._

## In a Field

Inside a [Field](?path=/docs/components-field--docs) the FieldLabel names the input and both buttons ("Increase Retention"), the FieldDescription and FieldError describe it, and the Field's `invalid`, `required` and `disabled` reach it, with no ids written by hand. The Field's `required` is announced; the NumberField's own `required` is the native constraint that also blocks an empty submit.

_Example: story `Stories.BoundInField`._

## Accessibility

- **A text box that says it holds a number.** The input is a textbox, so text editing works as in any field on every platform, with the role description "Number field" (the `numberField` message).
- **The buttons** are named "Decrease" and "Increase" (the `decreaseValue` and `increaseValue` messages), followed by whatever names the input: the FieldLabel inside a Field, or the `aria-labelledby` element ("Increase Retention"). A field named only by `aria-label` names them through the `decreaseValueFor` and `increaseValueFor` messages ("Increase Retention days"), so two fields side by side never have two buttons called "Increase". They are not Tab stops, because the arrow keys do the same; a touch screen reader reaches them by swiping. Each takes a 24px target under a coarse pointer, and a press with a mouse keeps focus in the input.
- **At a bound** a button is unavailable (`aria-disabled`), not only dimmed.
- **The wheel** never changes a value the reader is not working on: off by default, and with `allowWheelScrub` it steps only the focused field.

## Props

_Props: generated from `NumberField`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Example: story `Stories.Playground`._

_Rendered in the Storybook: Controls._

<!-- page: Components/Overlays (src/stories/components/Overlays.mdx) -->

# Overlays

Everything that floats over the page, from the smallest label to a full task. Four are anchored to the thing that opened them and four cover the page under a blanket. The anchored and modal overlays all use Base UI. Modal overlays manage focus and page scrolling; anchored previews keep focus on their trigger. The surfaces share one recipe, `elevation.surface.overlay`, `elevation.shadow.overlay`, the large radius, the enter and exit motion, so a product's overlays read as one family.

Each part has its own page: [Tooltip](?path=/docs/components-tooltip--docs), [HoverCard](?path=/docs/components-hovercard--docs), [Popover](?path=/docs/components-popover--docs), [DropdownMenu](?path=/docs/components-dropdownmenu--docs), [Dialog](?path=/docs/components-dialog--docs), [Sheet](?path=/docs/components-sheet--docs), [Drawer](?path=/docs/components-drawer--docs), [AlertDialog](?path=/docs/components-alertdialog--docs).

## Variants

| Need                                                             | Use              | Opens on                            | Closes on                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| A short label                                                    | **Tooltip**      | Hover or focus, after 300ms         | Leaving, Escape                        |
| A peek at a record: a few facts, no actions                      | **HoverCard**    | Hover or focus, after 600ms         | Leaving, Escape                        |
| A small task at its button: a filter, a reason, a picker         | **Popover**      | Click                               | Escape, outside click, Done            |
| A list of actions                                                | **DropdownMenu** | Click, Enter, Space, the down arrow | Choosing, Escape, outside click        |
| A focused task over the page                                     | **Dialog**       | The caller's state                  | Escape, the blanket, Cancel, the verb  |
| A modal selection, review or explicitly scoped parent-draft task | **Sheet**        | The caller's state                  | Escape, the blanket, the footer's verb |
| The bottom sheet, for a narrow screen and a quick task           | **Drawer**       | The caller's state                  | A drag down, Escape, the blanket       |
| A decision that needs a word before it happens                   | **AlertDialog**  | The caller's state                  | Cancel, Escape, the verb               |

_Example: story `Stories.Anchored`._

_Example: story `Stories.Modal`._

## Anatomy

- **The anchored four** sit beside their trigger, 4 to 6px off it, flipping when there is no room, with Tooltip adding a small arrow. A Tooltip is the dark one, `color.background.neutral.bold` with inverse text; the other three are the overlay surface with a hairline border.
- **The blanketed four** paint `color.blanket` over the page; nothing else paints it. Their surface is `elevation.surface.overlay` with `radius.xxlarge` (a Sheet has square corners, since it is an edge), a header with the title in `font.heading.xsmall`, a body part that scrolls (DialogBody, SheetBody, DrawerBody, AlertDialogBody), and a footer on `elevation.surface.sunken` with the buttons at the end. The title is the overlay's h2; headings inside start at h3.
- **Overlays record their surface.** The Dialog, Sheet, Drawer, AlertDialog, Popover and HoverCard popups set `utility.elevation.surface.current` to the overlay surface, so a sticky table header, a pinned cell or a scroll arrow inside paints the overlay's colour, not the page's.
- **The close** is one shared icon button at the top end, `dimension.control.small`. AlertDialog and Drawer compose explicit action buttons; a Drawer’s optional swipe handle is decorative.

## Accessibility

- **Focus moves in** when a blanketed overlay opens (Drawer focuses its popup by default; initialFocus can target an action or field) and **returns** to what opened it when it closes. The page behind is hidden from assistive technology and does not scroll.
- **Escape closes** every overlay. An outside click closes the anchored ones and the blanket closes a Dialog, a Sheet and a Drawer; an AlertDialog ignores it.
- **Pending holds.** `pending` on a Dialog, Sheet or AlertDialog cancels every request to close (Escape, the blanket, Close), disables the close controls while keeping them focusable (`aria-disabled`), so focus on one is kept, and marks the popup `aria-busy` until the command returns; PickerSheet's `pending` is its Sheet's. A Drawer cancels in its own `onOpenChange`.
- **A tooltip never holds a control**, a hover card never holds an action, a popover never holds a task the reader must finish.

## Style

- **One blanket at a time.** An AlertDialog may open over a Sheet or a Dialog, for the decision the task ends in; that is the only stack. Independent stacked record workflows should navigate or replace the current frame. A selection workflow owns its internal preview.
- **A sheet's next record is its next frame**, not a second sheet: the same surface, a Back chevron before the title (PreviewSheet's and PickerSheet's `onBack`), the stack in the URL so the browser's back agrees.
- **Anchored overlays stack on anything.** A Tooltip in a Dialog, a DropdownMenu in a Sheet, a Popover in a Drawer are fine; a Popover in a Popover is not.

_Example: story `Stories.Stacked`._

## Props

- **Trigger composition follows each component's API**: Popover uses `PopoverTrigger render={<Button />}`; DropdownMenu uses `DropdownMenuTrigger render` and `DropdownMenuContent`; Tooltip uses `TooltipTrigger render` and `TooltipContent`. HoverCard uses `HoverCardTrigger`, an anchor by default, with `render` for a custom link. Custom trigger components must forward their props and ref.
- **The blanketed four are opened by state**: `open` and `onOpenChange`. An act sets it; the caller clears it. Nothing opens a Dialog for the reader who did not ask.
- **Where the task lives decides the overlay.** At the button: Popover. An independent focused form: Dialog. Beside a usable list: Shell.Panel. A specifically modal selection or review task: Sheet. Under the thumb: Drawer.

## Content

- The blanket is `color.blanket`; nothing else paints it.
- A blanketed overlay's title is the act's verb (a Dialog), the record's name (a Sheet), or the question (an AlertDialog). Its primary button says the verb, never OK.
- What the reader must know is on the page or in the body, never only in a tooltip or a hover card.
- An overlay is never the record. The record has a page; the overlay is the way to it or the task on it.

## Sizes

Choose the smallest surface that fits the task. Dialog and Sheet take a `width` step (`small`, `medium`, `large`, `xlarge`, `fullscreen`) rather than pixels, so tasks of the same kind open at the same size; AlertDialog has `size`. Popover and HoverCard keep a runtime `style.width`. Content must reflow at a 320 CSS pixel viewport: the body part scrolls between a fixed header and footer, and in a window under 30rem tall the whole popup scrolls with the footer held in view. Check long titles, translated buttons, and browser zoom. A large task with navigation belongs on a page.

## States

Closed, open, pending, failed and completed are separate states. Keep the surface and draft open on failure and explain how to retry. A pending operation must settle or expose a recovery path. Close only after a successful command or an explicit cancel.

## Modifiers

Modal content takes Base UI's `initialFocus` and `finalFocus`. Base UI returns focus to the element that had it before the surface opened; pass `finalFocus` when that element goes away with the task, and move focus to a first field with `initialFocus`, never with `autoFocus`, which becomes the return target instead. `pending` on Dialog, Sheet and AlertDialog prevents dismissal while a command is in flight.

## Related

See Forms for validation and focus on error, Button for activation semantics, and Toaster for nonblocking completion feedback. Each overlay's page documents its exact dismissal contract.

## Don't

Do not rely on a toast as the only record of a failure, hide required instructions in a tooltip, nest independent modal tasks, or remove the opener without specifying a meaningful focus destination. Do not make a hover-only surface the sole route to an action.

<!-- page: Components/Pagination (src/stories/components/Pagination.mdx) -->

# Pagination

Navigation between pages using [shadcn’s flat Pagination parts](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/components/base/pagination). The caller owns page state, URLs and result counts.

## Anatomy

```tsx
<Pagination aria-label="Control pages">
  <PaginationContent>
    <PaginationItem>
      <PaginationPrevious href="?page=1" />
    </PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem>
      <PaginationLink href="?page=2" isActive>
        2
      </PaginationLink>
    </PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem>
      <PaginationEllipsis />
    </PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem>
      <PaginationNext href="?page=3" />
    </PaginationItem>
  </PaginationContent>
</Pagination>
```

Root is a nav, Content a list and Item a list item. Link uses a real anchor with the shared Button recipe. Base UI 1.7 Button adds button semantics even when rendered as an anchor, so Ledger preserves native link semantics here. Previous and Next are links with localized names, optional `text` and direction-aware icons.

_Example: story `Stories.Links`._

## Variants and states

`isActive` sets `aria-current="page"` and the selected appearance. All links accept native anchor attributes, events and refs, including href, target and rel. Ellipsis is decorative.

Previous and Next carry their words where the pagination has 384px of its own width and are arrows below it, named for a screen reader either way. The region measures itself, not the window, so the same pagination has words on a page and arrows in a 320px panel on the same screen. A pagination holding Previous or Next is a size container, so its width comes from where it sits, not from its links. It spans its container by default. At the end of a row, give it the rest of the row with `min-w-0 flex-1 justify-end`: its words show where that leaves 384px, and a narrower row shrinks it to arrows. Sized to its content instead (`w-auto`, an `auto` grid column), a pagination with words is 384px whatever its links need, so a longer list wraps inside it. Previous and Next read that width from their `Pagination` root; outside one they show arrows only. The list wraps rather than running past a narrow frame, and every link is at least 28px.

_Example: story `Stories.InANarrowPanel`._
_Example: story `Stories.AtTheEndOfARow`._

For in-memory tables, compose Button inside PaginationItem with native disabled and aria-current attributes. The internal DataTable pagination pattern owns page calculation, empty results and row-range text, using those same parts.

_Example: story `Stories.InMemoryTable`._
_Example: story `Stories.ManyPages`._

## Accessibility

Name each navigation region distinctly. Use links for URLs and buttons for local state changes. An unavailable link needs caller-owned semantics and activation handling; anchors have no native disabled attribute. Prefer omitting unavailable navigation links or rendering a disabled Button for an in-memory pager. RTL arrows follow the enclosing direction.

## Props

The configured `page`, `pageCount`, `onPageChange`, `total`, `pageSize` and `label` API is removed. Use native `aria-label` and explicit children. DataTable retains its page-size and table-state API; its internal composition preserves result counts and page controls.

_Props: generated from `Pagination`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._
_Props: generated from `PaginationLink`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._
_Props: generated from `PaginationPrevious`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._
_Props: generated from `PaginationNext`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

## Related

[DataTable](?path=/docs/patterns-data-table--docs), [Table](?path=/docs/components-table--docs), [Button](?path=/docs/components-button--docs).

<!-- page: Components/Popover (src/stories/components/Popover.mdx) -->

# Popover

An anchored dialog for controls, forms and supporting content. It follows shadcn's Base UI composition, with Ledger's surface, spacing and motion tokens.

```tsx
<Popover>
  <PopoverTrigger render={<Button />}>Review schedule</PopoverTrigger>
  <PopoverContent>
    <PopoverHeader>
      <PopoverTitle>Review schedule</PopoverTitle>
      <PopoverDescription>Reviews occur every quarter.</PopoverDescription>
    </PopoverHeader>
    <PopoverClose render={<Button />}>Done</PopoverClose>
  </PopoverContent>
</Popover>
```

## Composition

Root owns open state. Trigger and Close render native buttons by default; use `render` to compose Button, IconButton or FilterChip. Trigger's `nativeButton={false}` supports a custom element with button semantics. Custom components must forward their props and ref.

Content includes the portal and positioner. Native props, `ref`, `render`, and state callbacks for `className` or `style` apply to the popup. Title and Description connect their content to the dialog's accessible name and description; Header supplies their layout. When no visible title fits, give Content an `aria-label`.

Content paints the overlay surface and records it as the current one, so a child painted with `bg-surface-current` (a sticky list label, a pinned cell) matches the popover rather than the page. It defaults to 288px wide, `side="bottom"`, `sideOffset={4}`, `align="center"` and `alignOffset={0}`. Override width with `style={{ width: 300 }}` or match the trigger with `style={{ width: "var(--anchor-width)" }}`. The positioner handles collisions. Logical sides and alignment follow the Ledger locale; Content's `dir` can override it.

_Example: story `Stories.PopoverMatrix`._

## Focus and dismissal

Click, Enter or Space activates the trigger. Focus moves to the first tabbable control, or the popup if it has none. Touch opening focuses the popup to avoid opening a virtual keyboard. Content's `initialFocus` and `finalFocus` support explicit focus destinations.

The default `modal={false}` leaves the page reachable. Tab moves through controls and can leave the popup, dismissing it. Escape and Close dismiss it and return focus to the trigger; an outside press dismisses it while allowing the clicked control to receive focus.

For focus trapping, use Root's `modal="trap-focus"` and include `PopoverClose` inside Content. `modal={true}` additionally restricts outside interaction; see the upstream API for its scrolling behavior. Base UI 1.7 requires the Close part inside the popup to enable its focus trap.

Inside an existing Dialog, Sheet or Drawer, the popup stays within that surface's focus scope. Escape closes the popup first and returns focus to its trigger; a subsequent Escape can dismiss the enclosing surface.

_Example: story `Stories.Options`._

## Controlled tasks

Use `defaultOpen` for local initial state, or `open` and `onOpenChange(open, details)` for caller-owned state. `details.cancel()` rejects an open-state change. Keep form drafts in caller state when they should survive dismissal, and close after the task succeeds.

_Example: story `Stories.Task`._

## Migration and API

Replace the old `trigger` prop with `PopoverTrigger render`, move the body into `PopoverContent`, and replace `Popover.Close` with `PopoverClose render`. Move `label` to a Title or Content's `aria-label`; move placement and sizing onto Content. `width` becomes `style.width`, and `matchTriggerWidth` becomes `width: "var(--anchor-width)"`. State attributes follow Base UI, including `data-open`.

The flat parts retain their upstream props: [Root](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#root), [Trigger](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#trigger), [Popup](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#popup), [Title](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#title), [Description](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#description), and [Close](https://base-ui.com/react/components/popover#close). Content additionally exposes the four positioning props above; Header accepts native div props. See [shadcn's composition examples](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/components/base/popover).

_Props: generated from `PopoverContent`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

## Related

[FilterChip](?path=/docs/components-filterchip--docs) · [DatePicker](?path=/docs/components-datepicker--docs) · [Combobox](?path=/docs/components-combobox--docs) · [Dialog](?path=/docs/components-dialog--docs) · [Overlays](?path=/docs/components-overlays--docs)

# Progress

Based on [shadcn’s Base UI source](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/components/base/progress) and [Base UI](https://base-ui.com/react/components/progress). Ledger retains its tokens and application layouts.

## Anatomy

Task completion using Base UI Progress. Progress supplies its default Track and Indicator; ProgressLabel and ProgressValue are optional children. ProgressTrack and ProgressIndicator expose the corresponding native parts for custom composition under Base UI’s root. ProgressStacked remains the separate proportional coverage bar.

## Variants

_Example: story `Stories.ValuesAndRanges`._

_Example: story `Stories.LabelAndValue`._

_Example: story `Stories.StackedCoverage`._

_Example: story `Stories.CustomTrack`._

## Accessibility

Name meaningful bars through ProgressLabel or aria-label. Mark redundant decorative bars aria-hidden. Base UI keeps the indicator width, bounded value and accessible value in sync for min/max; null or a nonfinite value is indeterminate. Interactive stacked segments keep individual button names.

In forced-colors mode, system-color boundaries and fills keep tracks and progress indicators visible.

## Props

Progress exposes Base UI native root props and ref, including value, min/max, formatting, locale, render and state callbacks. Ledger tone and small/medium/large track sizes remain. Label, Value, Track and Indicator expose their corresponding native contracts.

### Migration and API

- Replace label with aria-label or ProgressLabel; valueText with aria-valuetext; showValue with ProgressValue children.
- Replace Progress.Stacked with ProgressStacked. Existing tone, size and coverage segment APIs remain.
- ProgressValue defaults to the formatted percentage; its children callback can display counts. Base UI performs clamping; the wrapper no longer calculates a second percentage.

<!-- page: Components/RadioGroup (src/stories/components/RadioGroup.mdx) -->

# RadioGroup

One selected value from a set of visible choices, using the shadcn Base UI composition. `RadioGroupItem` includes the circular indicator; labels and supporting content are composed outside it.

```tsx
<RadioGroup aria-label="Frequency" defaultValue="quarterly">
  <label className="inline-flex items-center gap-100">
    <RadioGroupItem value="monthly" /> Monthly
  </label>
  <label className="inline-flex items-center gap-100">
    <RadioGroupItem value="quarterly" /> Quarterly
  </label>
</RadioGroup>
```

_Example: story `Stories.RadioGroupMatrix`._

## Selection and layout

Use `defaultValue` for local state, or `value` and `onValueChange(value, details)` for controlled state. Selecting an item clears the previous selection; selecting it again keeps it selected. `details.cancel()` rejects a change. `disabled` blocks interaction; `readOnly` allows focus while keeping the selected value unchanged. Both props can apply to the group or an individual item.

The indicator is a 16px circle with an 8px dot. The selected circle uses Ledger's brand fill and a contrasting dot. The group defaults to a grid with an 8px gap. Use classes such as `flex flex-row flex-wrap gap-200` for a horizontal layout; there is no `orientation` prop.

Tab enters and leaves the group as one stop. All four arrow keys move focus and select, skipping disabled items and wrapping at the ends. Horizontal arrows follow the Ledger locale direction, which `dir` on the group can override. Space selects the focused item; Enter does not select it. Home/End and configurable focus wrapping are not part of the installed API.

_Example: story `Stories.Orientation`._

## Labels, Field and forms

The short path is a Field around a FieldSet: the FieldLegend names the group, the Field's hint and error describe it, and its `invalid` and `required` reach the group once. Each item is a horizontal Field with a FieldLabel, so it keeps its own name and needs no id. Invalid is the item's danger border, set once on the group; a focused item keeps the focus outline.

_Example: story `Stories.BoundInField`._

Outside a Field, name the group with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`; inside a FieldSet the legend names it. A wrapping label or a sibling label with `htmlFor` names each item and selects it when clicked, and `aria-describedby` links supporting text. `aria-invalid` on the group marks every item. Native `required` on RadioGroup makes its hidden radio inputs take part in browser and Base UI validation; the Field's `required` only announces and marks. A FieldSet's `disabled` disables the items.

`name` and `form` associate the hidden inputs with native submission. The selected item's value is submitted. Native form reset is caller-owned in Base UI 1.7: restore controlled `value` in the form's `onReset` handler.

_Example: story `Stories.InField`._

## Native props and composition

The group renders a div with `role="radiogroup"`. Each item renders a span with `role="radio"` and `aria-checked`, plus a hidden input. Item `ref` targets the visible control; `inputRef` and `id` target its hidden input. Group `inputRef` follows the selected input, or an enabled input when none is selected.

`render` composes a custom element and merges props, classes, styles and refs. An item rendered as a button uses `nativeButton` with `render={<button />}`; its `id` then targets the visible button. `className` and `style` accept Base UI state callbacks.

## Migration

Replace `RadioGroup.Item` with `RadioGroupItem`. Move label children and `description` into external labels and description elements. Replace `orientation="horizontal"` with layout classes. Selection values and callbacks use Base UI's generic value API, including the cancellable event details argument.

Each radio's boundary is `color.border.bold`, 3:1 against every surface, so an unchosen option can be found (WCAG 1.4.11). In forced-colors mode, the selected radio keeps a contrasting system-color dot and visible boundary.

_Example: story `Stories.Boundary`._

_Props: generated from `RadioGroup`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Props: generated from `RadioGroupItem`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

# Resizable

<ResizablePanelGroup>

_Example: story `Stories.Collapsible`._

Persist layouts where the composition needs it. Use the upstream `useDefaultLayout` hook, stable group/panel IDs and the hook’s `defaultLayout`/`onLayoutChanged` pair. Preserve an existing ID to read its saved layouts. Supply server-safe storage when rendering the hook on the server; the story demonstrates this explicitly.

The handle is a focusable separator with the orientation of the rule: a horizontal group has a vertical separator. Arrow keys resize; Home/End reach bounds; Enter toggles a collapsible panel. <!-- page: Components/Scroller (src/stories/components/Scroller.mdx) -->

# Scroller

A bounded scrolling region with an arrow at each edge that can still scroll. Select, DropdownMenu, Combobox and horizontal line Tabs compose it, so a long list and a wide strip scroll alike.

## Anatomy

`Scroller` is the bounded box: it sets `orientation`, how an arrow scrolls (`scrollOn`) and the `surface` the arrows sit on. `ScrollerViewport` is the element that scrolls; `render` substitutes a list (Combobox does), and `viewport` on the root points at an element the Scroller does not render (Tabs passes its ScrollArea viewport). `ScrollerArrow` renders one edge: `start` or `end`.

An arrow appears only when the viewport overflows, only at an edge that can still scroll, and only where the pointer can hover (`hover: hover` and `pointer: fine`); touch readers swipe and see none. While arrows show they replace the native scrollbar, and the viewport keeps their thickness clear as scroll padding, so a focused or highlighted item scrolls out from under them.

When a descendant receives keyboard focus, Scroller reveals it on its scrolling axis, including an item that was only partly visible. This moves its own viewport without scrolling the outer page; a nested Scroller handles its own focus reveal.

A horizontal strip keeps its current item in view: the selected tab (`aria-selected`), the current step (`aria-current`) or the pressed view (`aria-pressed`). The first time the strip overflows (on its first layout, or once late fonts or labels widen it), and whenever it narrows, that item scrolls back in if it ended outside, clear of the arrows. Focus does not move. Once it has overflowed, a strip that widens, or whose content changes, stays where the reader put it.

_Example: story `Stories.KeepsCurrentInView`._

## Vertical

Vertical scrollers scroll on hover unsaid: the arrow is a hover zone, hidden from assistive technology, and keyboard readers already move through the content. Menus use the `overlay` surface.

_Example: story `Stories.Vertical`._

## Horizontal

Horizontal scrollers step a page on click unsaid: the arrow is a labelled button outside the tab order that reads as one (a pointer cursor, a hover tint and a hairline on its inner edge), and it follows the locale's direction. Pass `scrollOn` to change either default.

_Example: story `Stories.Horizontal`._

## Composition

Select keeps Base UI's own scroll arrows, which step item by item and know the open method; they wear the Scroller arrow classes so the two cannot drift apart. Tabs sizes its arrows to the strip and gives them the strip's hairline. Do not add a second scroller, an overflow utility or a fade inside a part that already composes one.

## Props

_Props: generated from `Scroller`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Props: generated from `ScrollerViewport`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

_Props: generated from `ScrollerArrow`; the Storybook page and the package's `.d.ts` list them._

<!-- page: Components/SearchField (src/stories/components/SearchField.mdx) -->

# SearchField

One search input: the search icon, the query, and a clear button while there is a query. It narrows a list as the reader types, or runs a search on Enter. [Toolbar](?path=/docs/patterns-toolbar--docs) uses it for its search.

Use it wherever the reader finds or narrows records. Do not use it for a value the record keeps, such as a name or a reference: that is an [Input](?path=/docs/components-input--docs) in a [Field](?path=/docs/components-field--docs), which Escape and a clear button never erase. To pick one record from a list of options, use a [Combobox](?path=/docs/components-combobox--docs); to search the whole product, the [SearchDialog](?path=/docs/patterns-searchdialog--docs).

_Example: story `Stories.ClearAndEscape`._

## Keys and the clear button

| The reader               | What happens                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Types                    | `onValueChange` runs on every keystroke, as on Input.                                                                                       |
| Presses Enter            | Nothing, unless there is an `onSubmit`, which receives the query. Enter never submits a form around the field.                              |
| Presses Escape           | A query is cleared and focus stays in the field. With the field empty, Escape reaches whatever holds it: a dialog closes, a popover closes. |
| Presses the clear button | The query is cleared and focus goes to the field. The button shows only while there is a query and the field can change.                    |

Clearing sends the same input event typing does, so `onValueChange` receives `""`, native `onChange` runs, and a Field's dirty and filled state follow; `onClear` runs after it. A native form reset puts the default query back, and the clear button follows it. Enter or Escape that confirms or cancels an input method's composition is left to the input method, so cancelling a composition never erases the query. A caller's `onKeyDown` runs first, and `preventDefault()` in it skips the field's own handling of that key.

Enter never submits a surrounding form, with or without `onSubmit`, so a live filter inside a dialog's form cannot save the dialog when the reader presses Enter to search. The form's own primary still submits it.

_Example: story `Stories.InsideAForm`._
_Example: story `Stories.RunsOnEnter`._
_Example: story `Stories.InADialog`._

## Sizes and states

`medium` (32px) in a form, beside a medium Button; `small` (28px) in a toolbar, beside small buttons. `className` and `style` go to the field's frame, where its width is set; every other prop, the ref included, goes to the input. The value can be controlled (`value` with `onValueChange`) or not (`defaultValue`).

_Example: story `Stories.States`._

## In a Field

Inside a [Field](?path=/docs/components-field--docs) the FieldLabel names the search, the FieldDescription and FieldError describe it, and the Field's `invalid`, `required` and `disabled` reach it, with no ids written by hand. A disabled or read-only field has no clear button.

_Example: story `Stories.BoundInField`._

## Accessibility

- **A searchbox.** The input is `type="search"`, so it has the searchbox role, and `enterKeyHint="search"` puts a search key on a phone's keyboard.
- **Named.** By its FieldLabel, by `aria-label`, or else by its placeholder, and by the locale's "Search" when there is none. A placeholder that names what is searched ("Search controls") is enough in a toolbar; in a form, use a FieldLabel.
- **The clear button** is named "Clear search" (the `clearSearch` message). It is not a Tab stop, because Escape does the same from the keyboard, and a touch screen reader reaches it by swiping. Under a coarse pointer it takes a 24px target. Pressing it keeps focus in the field.
- **The icon is decorative**, hidden from assistive technology, and neither the frame nor the icon is a group: a screen reader meets one searchbox, not a searchbox inside unnamed groups.
- **Results are the caller's to announce.** The field does not know how many records matched; the list or table it narrows owns that result.
- **Landmark.** When this is the page's search, put it in a `<search>` element or a `<form role="search">`. Enter does not submit that form either, so run the search from `onSubmit` (or call the form's `requestSubmit()` there). A filter above a table is not a landmark.

The words it writes come from the locale (`search`, `clearSearch`), so a `LedgerProvider` translates them. Its spacing is logical, so right to left the icon sits at the right and the clear button at the left.

_Example: story `Stories.Localized`._
_Example: story `Stories.RightToLeft`._
